newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin sacks generals, courts Iran.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin sacks generals, courts Iran.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin sacked four senior generals on Friday in a move which could signal the start of a new crusade against corruption among Russian officials.

The Kremlin leader also took a decisive, if controversial line in foreign policy, joining his conservative foes in courting a visiting Iranian parliamentary chief despite a German judicial ruling that Tehran was behind state terrorism.

A presidential spokesman said Yeltsin, who declared war on graft as part of a new policy push this week, had dismissed Land Forces Commander General Vladimir Semyonov, and his deputy in charge of training, Colonel General Anton Terentyev.
The spokesman said Admiral Igor Khmelnov, chief of the navy's general staff and Vice Admiral Vyacheslav Kharnikov, First Deputy Commander of the Northern Fleet, had also been sacked.
He gave no reason for the sackings, but both Interfax and Itar-tass news agencies quoted sources as saying all four had been accused of "abuse of their official positions".
Semyonov was suspended in November after accusations of committing "actions incompatible with his post".
He has said he plans to sue Defence Minister Igor Rodionov who, he said, was behind his dismissal. Neither he, nor the other sacked generals were immediately available for comment.

The dismissals came a day after Yeltsin, trying to combat a policy drift which set in while he struggled with months of illness until early this year, launched a campaign against widespread graft, calling it a threat to the nation.

"Corruption is one of the main reasons that the authority of the Russian state is low today," Yeltsin said in a radio address on Thursday. "This is preventing us from bringing order to the country and threatening the very security of Russia.
"But I am determined, I have the political will and I have your backing in this fight," he added.
Top Russian officials have acknowledged that the web of bribery has penetrated every corner of life in the country and even reached the highest levels of government.
But many earlier attempts to fight the evil, some of them initiated by Yeltsin, have brought no significant results.

In a bid to show a firm hand in foreign as well as domestic policy, Yeltsin met the head of Iranian parliament, Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, and praised Russia's relations with Iran as Western nations distanced themselves from Tehran.
Germany expelled four Iranian diplomats on Thursday after a Berlin court announced its conclusion that Iran had ordered the 1992 murders of Kurdish activists in Berlin.
The European Union suggested after the verdict that member states recall their ambassadors from Iran "for consultations".
"We have good, positive co-operation with Iran, which shows a tendency to grow," Yeltsin told Nateq-Nouri in remarks sharply contrasting with the mood in Europe and the United States.

Russia has been seeking to diversify its foreign policy partners at a time when Western Europe is ignoring Moscow's protests and going ahead with plans to expand the NATO alliance into Eastern Europe.

The chairman of the State Duma (lower house), communist Gennady Seleznyov, told a joint news conference with Nateq-Nouri that the chamber did not differ with Yeltsin and his government on foreign policy, although they disagree on many other issues.
The Duma has no say in shaping Russia's foreign policy.

Seleznyov also issued veiled criticism of the German court verdict on Iran. "One can take a person to court for a crime he has committed but there is no court in the world which has the authority to carry out a sentence on a whole nation," he said.
